fact_label: Exchange control regime for foreign nationals and immigrants (SARB primary text)
value_raw: Foreign nationals temporarily resident in South Africa may, once foreign assets are declared on arrival: bank on a resident basis, freely invest/dispose of foreign assets, hold Non-resident Rand or foreign-currency accounts, and transfer accumulated South African funds abroad if the source is substantiated and the amount is reasonable relative to South African income-generating activity. Immigrants (permanent residents) get a parallel track: free disposal of foreign assets from arrival, and within 5 years of immigrating, the right to retransfer/re-export all introduced assets including growth. Resident South Africans have a R1 million/calendar-year single discretionary allowance plus a separate R10 million/calendar-year foreign capital allowance
date: 2026-01-07 (document version 1.69, circular 1-2026; directly fetched and read 2026-07-20)
notes: Closes the "direct SARB page fetch" gap flagged since 2026-07-18 ( close-out, bonus find beyond the row's own DHA scope). The document's own version-control table shows 69 revisions since 2016, most recent 2026-01-07 — a pattern of continuous incremental liberalization, not tightening or freezing. This specific guideline does NOT cover property-purchase exchange-control mechanics (e.g. the widely-reported "foreigner may finance up to 50% of a SA property purchase via local mortgage" rule) — that appears to live in a separate SARB Authorised Dealer Manual/circular, not yet directly fetched; real, narrower remaining gap, though a financing-detail question this project's own conventions treat as lower research priority than cash-purchase mechanics generally (see [on file]'s mortgage/financing-detail note). divergence_flag left at Not yet checked: no first-hand account of a foreign national actually executing one of these transfers was found this pass — the mechanism is primary-sourced, lived practice is not yet confirmed

fact_label: Table Mountain National Park — area and biodiversity
notes: Over 2,000 plant species within the park itself — more plant species than exist in the whole of the United Kingdom, per the park's own commonly-cited comparison. Forms part of the Cape Floristic Region and lies within the Cape Floral Kingdom, a globally-recognized biodiversity hotspot; Table Mountain's own range has the highest concentration of threatened species of any continental area of equivalent size in the world. Part of the UNESCO Cape Floral Region World Heritage Site. This criterion (Nature & water-adjacency) had zero fact rows before this pass despite being scored 4/5 in [on file] — this row and its two siblings below close that atomic-fact gap; the specialist's own red-flags.md files should be updated to cite these facts directly in a follow-up pass, not left as derived-only orphans

fact_label: Cape Floristic Region — UNESCO World Heritage status
value_raw: Over 9,000 vascular plant species, 69% endemic, in a region occupying under 0.5% of Africa's landmass yet holding ~20% of the continent's plant life; the smallest of the world's six recognized floral kingdoms. Cape Floral Region Protected Areas received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2004 (extended 2015), spanning ~1.09 million hectares across 8 protected areas
notes: Designated a biodiversity hotspot by Conservation International. Fynbos (the region's dominant Mediterranean-type, fire-prone shrubland biome) generates an estimated R77 million annually through wildflower harvesting and eco-tourism — a real, quantified local economic dimension to the nature access this criterion scores, not just a scenic claim

Monthly range 175.9 hours (June, deep winter) to 352.3 hours (January, peak summer) — a genuinely strong number of outdoor-usable daylight hours by any standard, directly relevant to "routine sustainability/pace of life" (the ability to build an outdoor-anchored daily routine year-round) even though it hadn't been captured as its own fact before this pass. This criterion (Routine sustainability/pace of life) had zero fact rows before this pass despite being scored 3/5 in [on file]

value_raw: Any person receiving income other than a standard employment salary (self-employed, freelance, business income) is automatically a "provisional taxpayer" under South African Revenue Service (SARS) rules — two advance payments required per tax year (within 6 months of the March tax-year start, and by end of February), based on estimated annual earnings, registered via SARS eFiling with an IRP6 return
notes: Directly relevant to the redefined "Income viability" criterion (per [on file]: not scoped to remote/passive income only — ceramics, a café, in-person tutoring are live possibilities too) — this is the actual compliance mechanism anyone earning non-salary income inside South Africa's tax-residency net would face, not previously captured as a fact row. This criterion had zero fact rows before this pass despite being scored 3/5 in [on file]. Only applies once SA tax residency is triggered (see the 183-day rule elsewhere in this file) — a foreign remote worker on a Remote Work Visa taxed only abroad under a Double Taxation Agreement would not be a South African provisional taxpayer at all; this row describes the mechanism for whoever does cross that line, not a universal requirement

Nearly 10 percentage points below the national unemployment rate — Cape Town holds South Africa's highest household incomes and lowest big-city unemployment rate, per the same source. Relevant context for the redefined Income viability criterion's local-economy dimension (would a small local business — a café, a tutoring practice — face a thin or a workable local customer/labor market): a real, if still elevated in absolute terms, local economic strength relative to the rest of the country, not an unambiguous positive on its own. Worth naming plainly: 23% unemployment is still high by global standards even as South Africa's best-performing major city
